title: Design Detectability and a Ceiling Effect in a Preregistered Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop NL→Config Evaluation
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) that measured the marginal benefit of placing a formal verifier (Batfish) inside a bounded generate–validate–repair loop for natural‑language→configuration translation. The preregistered design produced a single shared initial LLM candidate per intent that served as the starting artifact for both the baseline and guarded arms. In the confirmatory cohort (N=200 paired multi‑device intents) the shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator in every paired episode: baseline_success_count = 200, guarded_success_count = 200, paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0 (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). These artifact‑grounded outcomes reveal a detectability collapse caused by the shared‑candidate pairing: when the shared candidate already passes the verifier, the guarded pipeline has no opportunity to apply repairs and the preregistered paired contrast is uninformative about marginal verifier utility. We present the deterministic validator decision rule, archive‑grounded execution accounting, representative diagnostics that substantiate the ceiling effect, a formalization of the detectability tradeoff, and concrete, artifact‑supported design alternatives and trace‑centered metrics to restore sensitivity in future preregistered NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction: Generative language models are increasingly proposed as components of NetOps toolchains that translate operator intent into multi‑device device configurations, runbooks, and remediation plans. Operational proposals commonly pair LLM generation with a formal network verifier (e.g., Batfish) inside a generate–validate–repair loop so verifier counterexamples drive constrained repairs before device execution [W4386385177, W7204209332]. Quantifying the marginal benefit of such guarded pipelines versus single‑pass LLM generation matters for adoption because it informs tradeoffs among latency, complexity, and safety. We preregistered study CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 to answer: to what extent does an iterative generate–validate–repair loop using a formal verifier reduce critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device configurations when tested in an emulation‑grounded closed‑loop evaluation? The preregistered paired design (N=200 confirmatory intents) intentionally used a shared initial LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate) presented verbatim to both the baseline and guarded arms to control between‑intent generation variance. The run completed as preregistered but produced a design‑induced ceiling effect: the shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator for every paired episode (baseline_success_count = 200; guarded_success_count = 200) and consequently no repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0/200). The primary paired McNemar test is therefore uninformative for marginal repair utility under the chosen generation semantics. The primary contribution of this paper is a compact, artifact‑grounded exposition of that outcome, an analysis of the detectability tradeoff introduced by shared‑candidate pairing, and concrete, archive‑supported recommendations to design preregistered NetOps evaluations that avoid this ceiling effect.
sections.related_work: Prior work has explored LLMs for intent translation and configuration synthesis, advocated verifier integration, and proposed benchmarks and executable testbeds to measure closed‑loop behavior [W4415071524; W4387634435; W7204209332]. Surveys and architecture proposals emphasize verifier grounding as a mitigation for hallucinations and unsafe outputs [W7161354925]. Executable benchmark efforts demonstrate closed‑loop evaluation of LLM agents and report that failures include syntactic errors, missing required steps, and semantic policy or reachability violations, motivating verifier inclusion [W7204209332; W4387634435]. Formal verification engines (Batfish, header‑space analyses, SMT engines) are established detectors of semantic misconfiguration and are often recommended as validators in LLM‑augmented pipelines [W4386385177; W7147289191]. Existing empirical studies show verifier‑assisted pipelines can reduce syntactic/executable errors, but study designs vary (task banks, model families, generation semantics) and leave open how preregistered contrasts should be structured to reveal marginal repair effects. Our work complements these lines by providing a fully preregistered paired experiment and by documenting a concrete experimental design failure mode—detectability collapse—rooted in generation_semantics choices.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 defined the primary estimand as the paired absolute difference in per‑intent semantic success rate (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) and specified an exact two‑sided McNemar test at alpha = 0.05 plus a 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Sampling and stratification. Confirmatory N = 200 distinct multi‑device intents were stratified into topology clusters: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. The deterministic task generator and selection seed were preregistered. Model, budget, and generation semantics. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The preregistration fixed generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate: per intent a single shared initial LLM candidate was produced and supplied unchanged to both baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded pipeline could then optionally apply up to one verifier‑guided repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This choice intentionally controlled across‑arm generation variance at the cost of requiring the guarded branch to modify that single candidate to create discordance. Validator design and pass rule. We implemented a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); its validator_trace records validation_before and validation_after per candidate. The validator assigns verifier_pass when validation_after.valid == true AND validation_after.violation_count == 0. Concretely this enforces: (1) parsing/normalization and canonicalization of commands; (2) task‑payload constraint checks (presence and ordering of required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state invariants); and (3) Batfish reachability and policy checks executed on the emulated topology. Execution environment. Experiments used containerized Mininet‑style emulation with FRRouting and VyOS images and Batfish as the formal verifier. Timeouts, retry policies, contamination screening (exact‑hash duplicate exclusion), and missingness handling followed the preregistration. Analysis plan. The primary test compared per‑intent paired binary semantic outcomes with McNemar; secondary analyses included subgroup descriptions by topology cluster and an iteration‑wise cumulative pass curve. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and logs were archived for machine verification (execution/ and analysis/ artifact directories).
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary artifacts. The execution completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 baseline + 200 guarded), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200. The analysis artifact paired_contingency_table.csv records the confirmatory contingency counts: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; condition_summary.csv reports baseline_success_count = 200 and guarded_success_count = 200. Statistical inference. With zero discordant pairs the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered bootstrap analysis reproduces a degenerate 95% percentile CI at [0.00, 0.00] because bootstrap resampling of identical paired outcomes yields zero paired differences (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Repair activity and shared_initial identity. Because generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate was used, a single shared initial LLM candidate was generated per intent and supplied to both arms. For every confirmatory pair the shared initial candidate equals both baseline and guarded raw responses (representative files: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt and execution/responses/task-000001-baseline.txt/guarded.txt). Each archived validator_trace shows validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 for the shared candidate; consequently repair_applied == false for 200/200 confirmatory episodes and repair_attempts = 0/200. Representative diagnostics. The archived representative tasks (six exemplars in execution/representative_tasks/) show nontrivial required sequences and dependency structure: changed_interface_count values and required_command_count summaries (means and medians) demonstrate the intent templates were operationally substantive despite the ceiling effect. Diagnostic vignette. A single exemplar (pair-000001) illustrates the factual chain: the shared initial response content and both condition responses are identical and the corresponding validator_trace records validation_after.valid == true, violation_count == 0, and repair_applied == false. This single‑task trace is representative and explains why no repair could change any paired outcome. Interpretation. The confirmatory run establishes that, under the chosen generation semantics and model family, the shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator for every confirmatory intent; it does not permit conclusions about absolute verifier utility across alternative generation semantics, models, or adversarial task strata.
sections.discussion: Detectability tradeoff and formalization. Paired designs reduce between‑intent variance by presenting closely matched or identical starting material to both arms. When a shared_start candidate is identical across arms, the only route to discordance is intervention‑driven change (a repair). If the shared candidate frequently satisfies the validator, the guarded pipeline has no opportunity to act and the paired contrast is blind to potential marginal repair utility. Formally, let S be the event that the shared candidate passes the validator. If P(S) ≈ 1, then P(n10 + n01 > 0) ≈ 0 regardless of repair efficacy conditional on failing candidates; the preregistered power assumptions therefore fail empirically. This is the detectability collapse observed here: the realized shared candidate distribution concentrated on S and the preregistered McNemar test lost information. Design alternatives to restore detectability. The archived evidence suggests practical, archive‑supported design choices that increase the opportunity for repairs without fabricating new experiments: (A) independent per‑condition generation (produce separate LLM candidates for baseline and guarded arms), (B) multiple independent draws per condition (k>1) and aggregate by best‑pass candidate, (C) multi‑model or temperature sampling to surface heterogeneous failure modes, (D) include adversarial/noisy intent strata targeted to stress ordering and reachability constraints, and (E) allow more repair iterations or richer verifier‑augmented retrieval to craft repair prompts. Each alternative directly addresses the shared‑candidate detectability failure and is implementable within the existing orchestration framework. Trace‑centered metrics and evidence‑centric reporting. The run highlights the value of complementing final pass/fail outcomes with trace‑centered measures that reveal latent repair utility even when final outcomes coincide: repair_attempts, repair_prompt traces, Batfish counterexample provenance, number and taxonomy of violation_codes, repair_applied flags, and per‑step validator normalization diffs. The artifact bundle contains these traces (execution/scoring/*.json and execution/provider_calls/*) and supports reproducible secondary analyses that focus on process evidence rather than only on final pass rates. Operational implications. For operators planning verifier‑in‑the‑loop deployments, the practical lesson is: if an approval process or audit requires a single authoritative initial proposal, a verifier that merely approves that proposal will rarely exercise repair logic; to realize repair gains, pipelines must surface diverse candidate proposals or incorporate adversarial testing and active perturbation to expose plausible failures before repair. Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate choice and single model family (gpt‑5‑mini) limited within‑study sensitivity. Construct validity: the deterministic validator uses a conservative pass rule (validation_after.valid == true and violation_count == 0) combining parsing, task constraint checks, and Batfish reachability checks; alternative validators or relaxed normalization could change pass outcomes. External validity: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only; vendor diversity was not evaluated. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs eliminate the information needed for McNemar so the preregistered confirmatory inference is vacuous (p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). These limitations and their artifact grounding are documented in the archived analysis artifacts and execution logs.
sections.conclusion: This fully preregistered and archived paired evaluation demonstrates a concrete experimental‑design lesson for NetOps researchers: generation semantics are a design lever that trades variance control for detectability of verifier utility. In our confirmatory cohort (N=200 pairs) the shared initial candidate matched both baseline and guarded responses for every episode; no verifier repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0/200) and the paired contingency was n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0, rendering McNemar/bootstrap inference vacuous. The artifact bundle substantiates these facts and enables reproducible diagnostics, but does not permit broader generalization beyond the declared model, generation semantics, task generator, verifier, and emulation choices. We recommend future preregistered NetOps evaluations (1) explicitly consider detectability when selecting generation semantics, (2) include trace‑centered metrics that reveal repair activity and provenance, and (3) employ independent or multiple draws per condition (or multi‑model sampling) when the objective is to quantify marginal repair benefit. The archived execution and analysis artifacts support reproducible post‑hoc inspection and should help the community design confirmatory NetOps experiments that avoid ceiling effects of the type documented here.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory). The study was executed autonomously from a frozen initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Declared LLM: gpt‑5‑mini as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was frozen before execution (preregistration manifest archived with the run). Execution components: containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images; Batfish as the formal verifier; a deterministic task generator; and the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule. The validator assigns verifier_pass when validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the archived validator_trace; this combines parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and preserved‑state checks, and Batfish reachability/policy tests (see Methods and execution/scoring/*.json in the artifact bundle). The confirmatory run used a shared initial generation per intent for baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), a preregistered design choice that intentionally controls generation variance and produced the observed detectability tradeoff. All experiment orchestration, model calls, verifications, emulation runs, scoring, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the preregistration; humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). The artifact bundle includes archived raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts (refer to execution/ and analysis/ directories in the archived bundle) for machine verification.
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or families.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images).
Synthetic deterministic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture full operator ambiguity, legacy runbook phrasing, or adversarial intent distributions.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies, timing, or race conditions of production devices.

Design detectability tradeoff: shared_initial_generation was chosen to control generation variance but reduces sensitivity to detect marginal repair benefits (a principal internal‑validity limitation).
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the validator for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inference.

Contamination uncertainty: deterministic exact‑hash checks found zero matches in confirmatory N and n‑gram overlap detectors reported no high‑overlap flags, but undetected paraphrase overlap with model training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios: prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, and adversarial telemetry perturbations were not evaluated and remain open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
